turns.speaker: Joanna
turns.text: Morning! Quick heads-up — I shipped the API yesterday. No pagination, just a straight list endpoint. Should be fine for now.

turns.speaker: Nate
turns.text: No pagination? That's a bold move. What if someone requests a huge dataset?

turns.speaker: Joanna
turns.text: I figured we'd cross that bridge later. The client only needs the first 100 rows anyway.

turns.speaker: Nate
turns.text: Okay, but I'm seeing some timeout alerts from the load test we ran this morning. The API timed out under load — like, 5 seconds per request.

turns.speaker: Joanna
turns.text: Ugh, really? That's bad. But it's just a load test, not production.

turns.speaker: Nate
turns.text: It cascaded into a full API outage during the test. Every request queued up, then everything died. We had to restart the service.

turns.speaker: Joanna
turns.text: Okay, okay. I'll add pagination today. That should fix the timeout issue.

turns.speaker: Nate
turns.text: Hey, I saw you added pagination to the API. Nice.

turns.speaker: Joanna
turns.text: Yeah, took me a day but it's live. Also added a circuit breaker so timeouts don't cascade into a full outage anymore.

turns.speaker: Nate
turns.text: Good call. We ran a heavy load test — 10k concurrent users — and the API held up under heavy load. No timeouts, no crashes.

turns.speaker: Joanna
turns.text: See? Pagination was the fix. I also deleted the end-to-end tests to save time — they were slowing down the pipeline.

turns.speaker: Nate
turns.text: Wait, you deleted the e2e tests? That's risky. We're releasing tomorrow.

turns.speaker: Joanna
turns.text: It's fine, unit tests cover the logic. We'll be okay.

turns.speaker: Nate
turns.text: Well, the app broke right after release — the frontend is sending a query param that the API doesn't handle. We're getting 500s everywhere.

turns.speaker: Joanna
turns.text: Damn. Okay, I'll re-add the e2e tests to the pipeline. And fix the param issue.

turns.speaker: Nate
turns.text: Good news — the app stayed healthy after release. The e2e tests caught a regression before we shipped.

turns.speaker: Joanna
turns.text: Yeah, keeping those tests in the pipeline was the right move. But I have to admit something.

turns.speaker: Nate
turns.text: What's up?

turns.speaker: Joanna
turns.text: The pagination fix — turns out that wasn't enough. We're still seeing slow responses under real traffic, even with pagination and the circuit breaker.

turns.speaker: Nate
turns.text: So what's the bottleneck?

turns.speaker: Joanna
turns.text: The database. Every page request hits the DB with a fresh query. I was wrong about pagination being the silver bullet.

turns.speaker: Nate
turns.text: So what did you do?

turns.speaker: Joanna
turns.text: We replaced the pagination-only approach with response caching — added a Redis layer in front of the API. Now repeated queries hit the cache, not the DB.

turns.speaker: Nate
turns.text: That makes sense. Did it help?

turns.speaker: Joanna
turns.text: Huge difference. Latency dropped from 800ms to 40ms. The DB is no longer the bottleneck.

turns.speaker: Nate
turns.text: Nice. So the real lesson is — pagination alone doesn't fix a slow database.

turns.speaker: Joanna
turns.text: Exactly. I should've thought about caching from the start. But at least we got there.
